cards.h: A new sense for the universe
cards.b: For all of history we studied the universe with light. In 2015 we heard it for the first time: ripples in space-time itself. Combined with light, neutrinos and particles, this gives astronomers several 'senses' at once, called multi-messenger astronomy.

Einstein's general relativity (1915) says mass bends space-time. In 1916 he predicted that accelerating masses, such as two orbiting black holes, send out ripples that travel at the speed of light. Picture a heavy ball bouncing on a trampoline: waves spread out. The ripples stretch and squeeze space as they pass.

In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a binary pulsar whose orbit shrinks exactly as fast as relativity predicts if it loses energy to gravitational waves (Nobel 1993). The waves themselves were still unseen.

LIGO has two L-shaped detectors with 4 km arms in Hanford and Livingston, USA. Laser light bounces along each arm; a passing wave changes the arm lengths by about 10^-21 of their size, much less than a proton's width. On 14 September 2015, both detected GW150914: two black holes of about 36 and 29 Suns merging 1.3 billion light-years away. It was announced in February 2016. Weiss, Barish and Thorne won the 2017 Nobel Prize. Virgo (Italy) and KAGRA (Japan) joined the network.

On 17 August 2017, detectors heard GW170817, two neutron stars merging. Within 1.7 seconds a gamma-ray burst was seen, then telescopes worldwide saw a glowing kilonova in the galaxy NGC 4993. It showed that gravity travels at the speed of light and that such mergers forge gold and platinum.

Multi-messenger astronomy combines light, gravitational waves, neutrinos and cosmic rays. SN 1987A's neutrinos arrived hours before its light. In 2017 IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the blazar TXS 0506+056 together with gamma rays. Each messenger tells a different part of the story.

Pulsar timing arrays watch the ticks of millisecond pulsars. In June 2023 several teams (NANOGrav, EPTA, InPTA, PPTA) reported evidence of a low-frequency gravitational wave background, likely from supermassive black hole pairs. ESA's LISA space detector is planned for the 2030s to hear such mergers directly.

• 'LIGO sees waves like a telescope.' It listens; there is no image.
  • 'Gravitational waves are light waves.' They are ripples in space-time itself.
  • 'They are dangerous.' By the time they reach us, they are fantastically weak.

Indian scientists (IndIGO consortium, IUCAA, RRCAT, IPR) are members of the LIGO collaboration. LIGO-India, a third LIGO detector planned at Aundha in Hingoli district, Maharashtra, received government approval in April 2023. It will sharpen sky localisation of sources. The uGMRT and the Indian Pulsar Timing Array took part in the 2023 announcement, and AstroSat's CZTI searched for X-ray counterparts of GW events.

• Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time from accelerating masses, predicted in 1916.
  • LIGO detected the first on 14 September 2015 from merging black holes.
  • GW170817 combined waves with light and proved gravity travels at c.
  • LIGO-India and pulsar timing add Indian contributions.

Think about it: (1) Why do we need several detectors around the world? (2) What could waves tell us that light cannot?
